data.title: Appeals court slashes Alex Jones Sandy Hook judgment from $50M to $1.5M
data.description:
A Texas court on Friday cut the amount Infowars founder Alex Jones was ordered to pay to a family affected by the Sandy Hook shooting after they were subject to harassment when he claimed the attack was a hoax.

The Third Court of Appeals ruled unanimously to reduce the damages awarded to Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis from more than $45 million to $1.5 million, according to court documents. 

“The Court modifies the trial court’s judgment by reducing the exemplary damages award consistent with the statutory cap, resulting in exemplary damages awards of $750,000 to Scarlett Lewis and of $750,000 to Neil Heslin,” Chief Justice of the Third Court of Appeals of Texas Darlene Bryne wrote in her opinion Friday.

It found that there was no evidence that showed the harassment the couple endured from the claims Jones made allowed for the cap to be exceeded.

The ruling did not touch the $4.1 million Jones owes in compensatory damages to Heslin and Lewis, who lost their 6-year-old son in the shooting. Their son was among 20 children and six educators killed in the 2012 attack in Newtown, Connecticut.

On Friday, Jones said his legal team will continue to appeal the case to the state Supreme Court to get the remaining damages thrown out.

This ruling also does not affect the $1.25 billion Jones still has to pay to other families in Connecticut after he was found to be liable for harassment they endured when he claimed the mass shooting never happened. 

The Supreme Court in 2025 turned down Jones’s petition to avoid paying the sum which had plunged him into bankruptcy. 

Jones has yet to make any payments in either state as he continues to appeal the damage amounts and the attempt to liquidate his company, Free Speech Systems (FSS), which oversees Infowars. 

The Texas court in May had paused efforts made by satirical outlet The Onion from taking over FSS and Infowars. The deal would have given the outlet temporary authority and use of its trademarks. 

Jones has fought to retain control over the company and called the deal “illegal.”

data.title: Outbreak linked to alfalfa sprouts; people sickened with E. coli and Salmonella
data.description:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Friday that alfalfa sprouts are linked to a current E. coli and salmonella outbreak.

The agency has tied several food-borne illness cases to the consumption of alfalfa sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands, also urging Americans who have purchased the affected sprouts to throw them away or return them.

The contaminated alfalfa sprouts have sparked the third ongoing salmonella outbreak this month and second E. coli ongoing outbreak since the beginning of the year. In late July, the agency identified certain shelled eggs as a source of salmonella and later recalled some frozen blueberries for posing a severe risk of E. coli infection.

As of Friday, the CDC reported that the 55 reported cases were spread across 14 states, four of which resulted in hospitalization. While interviewing infected individuals, 76% had reported eating the sprout in the week before they got sick.

Most people impacted by the outbreak only contracted one of the illnesses — with 46 contracting E. coli and seven Salmonella. The remaining two caught both.

But the CDC estimates the number could be higher, as its common for those infected with salmonella and E. coli to recover without receiving medical care. 

The CDC believes to the outbreak began between May 31 and Aug. 8, and traceback data tied infections to alfalfa from Calco and Everything Sprouts — both sold at grocery stores and restaurants.

Cases in Minnesota and Wisconsin accounted for nearly 70 percent of recorded infections. The CDC traced back some of these cases to restaurants in both states that reported using Everything Sprouts-branded alfalfa.

Officials are still continuing to investigate this outbreak, which involves three different strains of E. coli and one strain of salmonella.

Salmonella is a common foodborne illness causing diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps. The CDC estimates that these symptoms can emerge between six hours and six days after infection and last four to seven days. 

Common symptoms of an E. coli infection are similar to salmonella but can also include stomach cramps, bloody stool or urine, vomiting and dehydration, according to the Food and Drug Administration. They can begin just a few days to as much as nine days after ingesting E. coli bacteria.

Investigators found the percentage of infected individuals who ate alfalfa was much higher than the number of Americans who report eating it, supporting their finding that the sprout caused the illness.

The CDC’s FoodNet Population survey — used to estimate how often Americans eat foods commonly linked to illness — found only 8.7 percent of respondents had eaten the sprout within the past seven days.

data.title: Reports of sexual assault in military dropped for third year in a row: Pentagon
data.description:
Reports of sexual assault in the U.S. military dropped for the third year in a row in 2025, and the Pentagon received a slightly lower number of sexual harassment complaints last year compared to 2024, the department said in a new report that was made public on Friday. 

The Pentagon received a total of 7,998 reports of sexual assault in 2025, down from the previous year’s 8,195 reports. There were 8,515 reports of sexual assault in 2023 and 8,942 reports in 2022. 

Out of the 7,998 reports in 2025, 5,022 were unrestricted reports and 2,976 remained restricted at the end of Fiscal Year 2025, the Pentagon said in the 29-page report. 

Unrestricted reports for sexual harassment or sexual assault are reported to the chain of command and it results in an official probe, allowing service members to access mental health care and legal assistance. 

“Dignity, respect and discipline are foundational to the warrior ethos and the overall preparedness of the force. Sexual assault and sexual harassment undermine these values, eroding trust and threatening the mission,” Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony J. Tata said in a statement. 

“The FY 2025 report underscores our ongoing commitment to maintaining high standards, protecting our people, and building a unified, ready and lethal fighting force,” Tata said.

During 2025, the Pentagon received 2,936 sexual harassment complaints, a bit lower than in 2024 when the department got 3,014 complaints. 

The Pentagon is obligated to send an annual report to Congress as outlined in Section 1631 of the 2011 Ike Skelton National Defense Authorization Act. The 2025 report was delivered to the Senate and House Armed Services Committees, along with the House and Senate Veterans Affairs panels on Aug. 10. 

The Marine Corps had the highest percentage of women experiencing unwanted sexual contact among service branches with 6.4 percent, followed by 5.1 percent in the Navy and 4.5 percent in the Army. The Air Force was the lowest at 2.8 percent. 

Among men, the Navy was the highest at 1.5 percent in 2025. Army and Marine Corps were at 1 percent, the report said. 

The Pentagon said the estimated rate of unwanted sexual contact for active-duty women fell from 6.8 percent in 2023 to 4.3 percent in 2025. A third of victims came forward last year, an increase from a quarter in 2023. 

“This statistically significant decrease in estimated prevalence was mostly driven by fewer enlisted women (E1-E4 and E5-E9) and junior officer women (O1-O3) as well as women ages 35 and younger indicating past-year unwanted sexual contact on the survey,” the department wrote in the report. 

About 1 percent of active duty men indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact in 2025, a slight decrease from 2023 when it was at 1.3 percent. 

Around 20,492 active service members, 9,860 active duty women and 10,632 active duty men, experienced unwanted sexual contact last year, a drop from 2023 when 29,061 active duty said the same. 

Outside groups pointed to the 2025 figure being nearly 40 percent higher than in 2016, when it was 14,900 and last year’s numbers being roughly identical to 2018, with 20,500. 

About a third of service members who indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact last year reported their incident to their authority, an increase from 25 percent in 2023. 

The Pentagon had “sufficient” evidence to take disciplinary action in 1,321 cases of individuals probed for an allegation of sexual assault, the department said in the report. 

Josh Connolly, the senior vice president of Protect Our Defenders, a nonprofit group that works to end sexual misconduct in the military, said he would not take the Pentagon’s figures at “face value” and neither should the public. 

“Survivors are more afraid to come forward than they were two years ago, and this administration has spent the past year giving them reason to be – rolling back whistleblower protections, making it harder to report anonymously, warning people who come forward that they may be punished for it,” Connolly said in a statement on Friday. “A number that falls because people stopped talking is not progress.” 

Early last year, the Navy halted sexual assault prevention and response training. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in October last year that he would revamp offices with the Pentagon’s inspector general office and the department’s equal employment opportunity office that allowed service members to anonymously file whistleblower complaints. 

“Talk to those who do report,” Connolly said on Friday. “The vast majority of those cases go nowhere. Documents get lost. Evidence never gets used. They’re handed from one lawyer to the next, or never get one at all. Then they’re pushed out and lose their medical and mental health care on the way.”

data.title: TikTok reaches $400M settlement with DOJ over alleged children's privacy law violations
data.description:
TikTok and its parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay $400 million to settle with the Department of Justice (DOJ) over allegations the platform violated a children’s online privacy law, the agency said Friday.

The company will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million after a court dismisses an earlier consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, known as Musical.ly, according to the DOJ.

The DOJ sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024, accusing the video-based social media app of violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). The law bars online platforms from collecting data on users under 13 years old without their parents’ consent.

The government alleged that the company allowed kids under 13 to create accounts and failed to delete their accounts and information when asked by parents.

“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said in a statement.

“The Department’s priority is ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations,” he continued. “This resolution secures a substantial recovery while reinforcing the protections that families expect and deserve.”

The Hill has reached out to TikTok for comment.

The DOJ noted in a press release that TikTok has “undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices” since it brought the lawsuit two years ago.

The platform is now under the control of TikTok USDS Joint Venture, an entity that is majority owned by American investors, after Congress passed a law in 2024 requiring ByteDance to divest from the app or face a U.S. ban.

The push for the divest-or-ban law stemmed from national security and privacy concerns about ByteDance’s ties to China. President Trump repeatedly pushed back the deadline to enforce the ban after taking office, as he sought to strike a deal with Beijing to keep the app available in the U.S.

Trump signed off on a deal to turn over TikTok to the joint venture last September. ByteDance maintained a 19.9 percent stake in the company, while Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX each received a 15 percent stake and are considered managing investors.

data.title: Controversial attorney Ed Martin leaving Justice Department
data.description:
The head of the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group, Ed Martin, is leaving the department, capping a chaotic tenure in the Trump administration.

Martin, who also served as the U.S. Pardon Attorney, has been at the center of a string of controversies since the earliest days of joining the administration, including failing to advance as a nominee for U.S. Attorney for D.C.

“Ed Martin has been with me from the very beginning, and done an incredible job as an Attorney, Director of the Weaponization Working Group, and the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia,” President Trump wrote on his social media site announcing the departure.

“Ed is now leaving to go outside to fight Legal Battles for the upcoming Midterm Election, and the Presidential Election of 2028. I know he will do an outstanding job, ensure Free, Fair, and Honest Elections, and strongly advance our Constitutional Rights.”

“Proud to serve. Fight Fight Fight,” Martin wrote on X in response to the news.

Martin had failed to gain the support of Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) as he had represented numerous clients who had stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

While serving as acting U.S. attorney while his nomination was pending, Martin moved to dismiss some cases of clients — sparking calls for an inquiry into the apparent conflict of interest by the D.C. bar that has since been taken up by its Office of Professional Responsibility.

“By not recusing himself from this matter, Mr. Martin created an impermissible conflict of interest and appearance of impropriety by using his new government office to favor his client, whom he was defending from the very charges he sought to dismiss,” Sen. Dick Durbin (Ill.), the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, wrote in a 2025 letter requesting an ethics investigation.

Martin made a number of notable moves in just a few months in the acting role, such as sending letters to two sitting Democratic lawmakers informing them they were under investigation for past comments he alleged were threatening, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

He also sent a letter to Georgetown University saying he would not hire any interns or attorneys from the school if they did not end their diversity, equity and inclusion policies, later escalating that threat by saying failure to respond would “bear directly” on its nonprofit status. That matter is also under investigation.

DEVELOPING…

data.title: Navy reportedly weighs renaming aircraft carrier for Trump
data.description:
WACO, Texas (KWKT) — The name of Pearl Harbor hero Doris Miller could be removed from one of the U.S. Navy’s next aircraft carriers, with President Trump’s name reportedly among those being considered as a replacement.

The Navy has been discussing renaming the future USS Doris Miller, the Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier designated CVN-81, reports CNN. No decision has been formally announced.

The carrier was named for Miller in January 2020 during a ceremony at Pearl Harbor.

At the time, Acting Secretary of the Navy Thomas Modly said the selection recognized not only Miller, but generations of enlisted sailors.

“In selecting this name, we honor the contributions of all our enlisted ranks, past and present, men and women, of every race, religion and background,” Modly said.

The naming was historic. The USS Doris Miller would become the first U.S. aircraft carrier named for a Black American and the first named in honor of a sailor for actions performed while serving in the enlisted ranks.

Miller was born in Waco, Texas, on Oct. 12, 1919, and joined the Navy in 1939. He was serving aboard the battleship USS West Virginia when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941.

During the attack, Miller helped wounded sailors before manning an anti-aircraft gun and firing at Japanese planes, despite having no formal training on the weapon.

Miller was later awarded the Navy Cross for his actions, becoming the first Black American to receive the decoration.

Miller was killed in action in November 1943 when the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay was torpedoed and sunk during operations in the Pacific.

The Navy has also honored Miller before. The Knox-class frigate USS Miller entered service in 1973 and remained in commission until 1991.

Sources told CNN discussions of renaming the USS Doris Miller have been underway for months, with the ship increasingly referred to internally by its hull number, CVN-81.

The sources, which spoke to CNN anonymously, said Trump’s name is among those under consideration if the carrier is renamed.

Miller’s family told CNN they were not informed in advance about the possibility of his name being removed from the ship.

Official Navy historical records continue to identify CVN-81 as the future USS Doris Miller.

Nexstar’s KWKT reached out to the U.S. Navy’s Office of Information, who has said they do not have anything to share at this time.

data.title: Appeals court affirms top federal prosecutor in Albany 'not lawfully serving'
data.description:
A federal appeals court panel ruled Friday that John Sarcone III was “not lawfully serving” as the top federal prosecutor in upstate New York when he subpoenaed Attorney General Letitia James’ (D) office last year.

The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Sarcone’s January disqualification as the acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York in a 2-1 decision, affirming a lower court order that also quashed the subpoenas.

The ruling is yet another blow to the Justice Department’s efforts to test the limits of federal vacancy law and bypass Senate confirmation.

“We hold that Sarcone was not serving as Acting U.S. Attorney when he obtained the subpoenas because the FVRA [Federal Vacancies Reform Act] permits only a First Assistant already in place when the vacancy arises to become the acting officer automatically,” Judge Guido Calabresi wrote in a 39-page opinion.

Calabresi, a Clinton nominee, was joined in the majority by Biden appointee, Judge Maria Kahn. Judge Michael Park, nominated during President Trump’s first term, dissented.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department told The Hill Friday that they disagree with court’s decision and “intend to take this case to the Supreme Court.”

The FVRA states the first assistant to any Senate-confirmed officer assumes the acting role by default whenever a vacancy occurs.

The Trump administration has sought to leverage the automatic succession rule to install top federal prosecutors by designating individuals as first assistants — the No. 2 role in the U.S. Attorney’s Office — or, in some cases, simply delegating them the powers of the job.

But the 2nd Circuit majority found both of those maneuvers to be unlawful.

“To install someone in a vacant office through a general delegation authority that [federal statute] expressly forbids, is to install an acting officer by another name,” Calabresi noted. “The FVRA forbids it”

After Sarcone’s 120-day term as interim U.S. attorney expired last July, district judges in New York declined to appoint him to the role indefinitely. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently changed his title to “special attorney”, allowing him to remain in the acting position.

Last August, Sarcone subpoenaed James’ office for information about its civil fraud investigation against President Trump and his business and another case involving the National Rifle Association.

U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield blocked the subpoenas in January and disqualified Sarcone, finding that the DOJ’s workaround violated federal law.

Park disagreed with Friday’s ruling, arguing in a 24-page dissent that Sarcone was legally authorized to seek the grand jury subpoenas.

“By concluding otherwise, the majority imposes new limits on executive authority, upsetting the balance that Congress struck in the FVRA,” the Trump appointee wrote.

The 2nd Circuit’s decision follows a series of recent appeals court rulings that have invalidated the Trump’s administration’s attempts to install loyalists as the lead federal prosecutors in California, Nevada, New Jersey and elsewhere.

data.title: US ambassador to Belgium criticizes Ghent University's suspension of professor over Jason Arday accusations
data.description:
U.S. Ambassador to Belgium Bill White on Friday condemned the decision made by Ghent University to suspend researcher Nathan Cofnas over his plagiarism accusations against Jason Arday.

White said on social platform X the decision made by the university to put Cofnas under investigation was “retaliation against an American scholar following his accurate whistleblower reporting on academic fraud.”

The ambassador also announced, “we are therefore reviewing any relationships we have with Ghent University.”

“Dishonest, corrupt institutions that engage in, or reward, scapegoating mob behavior are not desirable partners for us,” White stated.

Arday was in the news in 2023 when Cambridge University hailed him as the youngest Black professor in the institution’s history. Three years later, Arday was accused in the news of plagiarizing his academic work, which he denied. 

He was found dead Aug. 14 in his South London home. 

Cofnas, a former Cambridge researcher who left the university after his remarks about diversity programs and minorities sparked widespread protests, said in a July 21 article that he had found evidence of Arday’s plagiarism.

“Many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source,” he wrote about Arday’s 2015 dissertation.

He continued in the article that retired Plymouth Marjon University professor Dave Harris had raised concerns about Arday allegedly plagiarizing subsequent academic articles, which caused two academic journals to issue corrections.

Ghent University notified the public Thursday that a staff member was under “preliminary disciplinary investigation” and had been suspended as a precaution. The university declined to give details “in order to safeguard the confidentiality of the personnel file and the disciplinary proceedings.”

Cofnas said Thursday on social media he was under investigation by Ghent University “for discriminating against Arday.”

Rector Petra De Sutter and Vice-Rector Herwig Renaert shared in a statement on Thursday about Arday’s death that “Ghent University stands for respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism.”

“We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited,” they said.

Ghent University did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

data.title: HHS launches autistic missing persons alert initiative
data.description:
The Department of Health and Human Services announced on Friday a new federal initiative to improve preparedness and response when autistic individuals are reported missing. 

The agency will partner with the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to strengthen coordination among emergency management agencies, law enforcement, first responders, and community partners nationwide. 

Called the National Autism Missing and Endangered Person Alert Initiative, HHS said it reflects a shared federal commitment to treat high-risk, autism-related missing-person cases with appropriate urgency. 

“When an autistic child or adult goes missing, every minute matters,” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. “President Trump has made improving the lives of Americans with autism and their families a priority. We are bringing federal, state and local partners together to improve prevention, speed the response, and help bring autistic children and adults home safely.” 

HHS said it will also establish a national framework of best practices for autism-related missing person cases, which will aim to address the leading causes of preventable injury and death among autistic individuals, like accidental drowning. 

The initiative will build on existing missing and endangered person alert capabilities “that gets critical information to authorities and the public quickly and helps bring missing persons home safely,” Kennedy said during a press conference.  

“Alert faster, search smarter and save lives,” he added. 

But Kennedy stressed HHS has only just started to design a framework; the system doesn’t exist yet. 

“If an autistic loved one goes missing, people should call 911 immediately. And be ready to share critical information about communication, behavior, about the attraction of water,” Kennedy said.  

Approximately half of autistic children engage in wandering behavior at some point, HHS said.  

Drowning accounts for the majority of autism wandering fatalities, and many missing individuals are found close to their last known location.  

The National Autism Safety Council reports that an average of eight autistic children die each month in the U.S. following wandering or elopement, most often from drowning in nearby water.

data.title: Live updates: Trump lifts beef import tariffs, heads to South Carolina to rally for Graham
data.description:
President Trump on Friday sought to ease price pressure on beef prices by temporarily lifting the tariffs on imported beef. The move drew swift and sharp rebukes from some lawmakers and ranchers.

Trump is set to hit the campaign trail Friday in an attempt to give Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) one last boost before the special GOP primary runoff Tuesday.

Graham, a political newcomer who replaced her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), is going up against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) for the opportunity to snag the Republican seat in the Palmetto State.

Darline Graham’s inexperience showed on the debate stage Tuesday when she was unable to answer a national security question, raising uncertainty about her ability to serve in the Senate.

The Supreme Court on Friday temporarily halted an appeals court order that would’ve stopped above-ground construction on the White House ballroom. Chief Justice John Roberts’s administrative stay gives the court additional time to consider the administration’s emergency appeal but contains no explanation. It does not necessarily reflect the court’s thinking on the underlying legal issues.

IndyCar will take over the District of Columbia this weekend, with the Freedom 250 race Saturday and Sunday. It may cause a “little bit of carnage,” the IndyCar chief said.

Follow live below.
